summary:
The shortest book in the New Testament: thirteen verses, about the capacity of a single sheet of papyrus. It comes from "the elder" to "the elect lady and her children" — possibly a woman who hosted a house church, though most scholars read the lady as a congregation addressed under a figure. The situation is the one behind 1 John: traveling teachers were circulating who denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, and the elder writes ahead of them.

The letter holds two commands together. Love one another — not a new commandment, the elder notes, but the one they have had from the beginning. And do not host the deceivers: "do not receive him into your home or even greet him" (v. 10). The second command needs its background. Traveling teachers in that world depended on local believers for food, lodging, and an audience, so hospitality was sponsorship; to take a false teacher in was to fund and amplify the teaching. The elder's judgment is that this is not love but complicity.

Read the letter as a community learning discernment in real time: truth and love are not rivals here, and the elder refuses to give up either one.
